book: 077 - Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book

chapters.relation: The editors' introduction argues that Boardwalk Empire's Prohibition setting - bootleggers, corrupt politicians, G-men, and ordinary citizens at one table against the Volstead Act - puts its characters in philosophically loaded situations that bear directly on real life. It then maps the volume: Littmann reads Nucky as a Machiavellian Prince, Greene casts him as Nietzsche's Superman, Archibald reads Gillian through Plato, Brace and Kingsbury test Aristotle's happiness against Nucky, Chalky, and Margaret, and Robison-Greene treats Jimmy and Richard as war veterans facing existential problems. It closes by previewing chapters on Van Alden's God, the ethics of lying (Fallis), storytelling (Carveth) and deception (Cobb), the body politic (Schwanebeck) and the social contract (Fitzpatrick), causing versus allowing harm (Da Silva), violence (Mellamphy), and a Freudian reading of Jimmy and Gillian (Hirschbein).

Littmann tests The Prince against the real bosses behind the show - Nucky Johnson, Capone, Luciano, Rothstein, Torrio - and argues that Prohibition-era history bears out Machiavelli's rules of power. Seizing new opportunities pays (Nucky turning Atlantic City into the World's Playground, Colosimo gunned down for refusing bootlegging, Luciano eliminating Masseria and Maranzano to modernize the Mafia), and harming a rival without crushing him invites revenge (Nucky's fatal leniency toward Jimmy, Maranzano leaving the scarred Luciano alive). A ruler needs good arms, must tailor appearances to each audience (Capone's banquet murder of Anselmi and Scalise, Nucky's respectability and staged generosity), and above all must avoid hatred - the downfall of Nucky, Capone, and Luciano, and of the needlessly arrogant Rothstein, shot over a gambling debt he could easily have paid.

Greene asks whether Nucky is Nietzsche's Ubermensch and works through each criterion. Nucky, Gyp Rosetti, and the other mobsters are passionate, active shapers of their world (Van Alden fails here), and Nucky is a genuine creator of values after the death of God - his whopper to the Temperance League, his flip-flopping sermons to black and white congregations, and his 'I. Am. Not. Seeking. Forgiveness.' over Jimmy's body reject slave morality where the other gangsters merely follow the objective moral code of omerta. He sacrifices lesser lives (Hans Schroeder, Gillian) and has the required dark side, but he fails the final test of teaching the eternal recurrence, so he remains only 'well on his way' to Superman - a status the show's women (Margaret, Lucy, Gillian) never approach, hovering closer to the last man.

Hirschbein has Freud analyze the audience first: like Van Alden, the repressed hypocrite whose true self erupts in drowning Sebso and burning his workplace tormentor, we watch Nucky and Jimmy as avatars of our own repressed aggression and lust. Freud's contest of Eros and Thanatos - his reframing of Plato's tripartite soul as id, ego, and superego - explains why civilization demands renunciation while spectacle like Boardwalk supplies vicarious gratification, with Milgram's and Zimbardo's experiments showing how thin the civilized veneer is. Jimmy's seduction by his mother and killing of the Commodore enact the Oedipus complex writ large, Freud's primal-horde story of the sons' parridical revolt against the father, and the show's catharsis is what lets us live with the sin.

Brace and Kingsbury use the Nicomachean Ethics to argue that Nucky, Chalky, and Margaret mistake pleasure and the mere instruments of happiness - tailored suits, money, useful connections, the appearance of virtue - for Aristotle's stable, self-sustaining virtuous activity, so their lives stay unstable and empty. Nucky 'buys' even Jimmy and Margaret, Chalky's jail-cell staging with David Copperfield shows how fragile his facade of cultivation is, and Margaret's acquisitions end in blackmail and in bribing God over Emily's polio. Only Richard Harrow, the Tin Man whose collage-clippings represent a happiness he believes he can never have, moves toward real Aristotelian friendship through Jimmy's 'Of course I would; right down to the last bullet' - the philia Aristotle calls most necessary for a happy life.

Carveth argues that the show's historical license is ethically troubling because docudrama viewers - especially those who know nothing of 1920s Atlantic City - absorb 'reel history' as fact. He documents the blend of real and invented: Buscemi's slight Nucky Thompson against the imposing real Nucky Johnson, a fictional military past for Capone, Torrio stripped of his mentor role, and the McGarrigle episodes' misrepresentation of de Valera, Collins, and the Anglo-Irish Treaty. The deepest distortion is violence - the real Nucky ruled through jobs, ostracism, and economic coercion rather than murder, but that would not make good television - and given research showing viewers 'learn' from docudramas they know least about, Terence Winter's ninety-percent-accuracy claim amounts to an unethical misleading of the audience.

Sirvent and Baker take Van Alden's 'strong providential theology' - 'his fate rests in God's hands' at the burned Agent Clarkson's bedside - as a live version of the problem of evil, traced through Augustine and Aquinas to Calvin's all-determining divine omnipotence. The Arminian free-will escape leaves God like a parent watching a child run into traffic, and the 'mysterious ways' reply makes God's moral vocabulary so alien that a God who burns his beloved is 'one-sided' and unworshipable - the same theology that lets Van Alden shift blame for Lucy's pregnancy onto a 'charge from God' before drowning Sebso as 'the judgment of the wicked.' They close with Nucky's God, an inner impetus toward good that asks rather than coerces, and with process theology's persuading God, while Gyp Rosetti's Easter rant at the crucifix shows what believing in the omnipotent alternative costs.

Da Silva asks what Nucky deserves for bringing the thirteen-year-old Gillian to the Commodore and failing to stop the rape, and whether Jimmy - whose very existence depends on that wrong - is entitled to blame him and to ally with the worse man. Working through the doing, enabling, and allowing harm distinction with euthanasia and Good Samaritan cases, degrees of blame, and Parfit's point about collective action, he argues Nucky did wrong but likely less wrong than the Commodore, while Jimmy can blame on his mother's behalf and need not regret a birth that was still good for him - against Benatar's antinatalism. Jimmy's coup fails him, but the moral reason behind it, Nucky's contribution to the rape, was genuine.

Fallis sorts Atlantic City's lies to show which are wrong and why. Kant's and Augustine's absolute bans go too far and Grotius's life-saving exception does not apply - most of these lies get people killed - yet even altruistic lies (Margaret for Madame Jeunet and the ledger), lies told to those who want to be deceived, lies to liars, and Sorensen's bald-faced lies that no one believes (Jimmy's flat movie alibi, Rothstein's 'skilled player' whopper) remain wrong: they take informed choice out of the victim's hands, violating the Kantian autonomy that grounds the wrong of lying, and they corrode the trust on which even criminals' co-operation depends.

Schwanebeck reads Nucky's fastidious grooming and Prohibition's purity crusade through the body politic metaphor: from Cicero and Seneca's De Clementia, where head and body of the state depend on each other, through Hobbes's bearded Leviathan frontispiece, to temperance propaganda that framed alcohol as poison entering the national bloodstream and wartime posters demanding 'a clean America.' The show exposes the purity ideal as illusion - the true purists are the Klan massacring Chalky's men and the hand-washing Van Alden shouting 'Let these waters wash you clean!' over Sebso's drowning body. Nucky rules less like Seneca's genuinely clement emperor than like Machiavelli's prince who merely appears virtuous, and the gangster genre's kingly tropes ('Et tu, Eli?') crown him head of Atlantic City's body politic.

Robison-Greene reads the returning soldiers through Camus and Sartre. War reveals the absurd - Jimmy's Argonne story of the German soldier who would not die even in a hopeless situation strips life of inherent value - and Van Alden's fervent Christianity is the escapist response to absurdity, bad faith that denies his own desires. Jimmy and Richard are trapped in bad faith over facticity and transcendence, Richard pinned by 'the look' of a community that only sees his ruined face ('Hell is other people'); neither fully becomes an absurd hero like Meursault, since Richard still craves meaningful ties, but Jimmy finally embraces the absurd at the War Memorial, arranging his own death with the calm of a man who 'died in the trenches, years back.'

Fitzpatrick uses the social contract tradition to explain Prohibition-era Atlantic City. Hobbes's state of nature fits the gang warfare left where no Leviathan is strong enough to enforce federal law against Nucky; Locke's fits a night-watchman government overreaching into Prohibition and thereby breaking the contract, as with Nucky's illegitimate protection 'taxes'; Rousseau's noble savage corrupted by commercial society fits the Klan's pleasure in cruelty and innocent Tommy set against scheming adults. Ethical egoism frames Nucky's framing of Hans Schroeder, consequentialism the Temperance Union's cost-benefit failure, and deontology Margaret's lying campaign speech, while Marx's and Mill's view that human nature is malleable explains the season-spanning transformation of Nucky from half-gangster into 'a gangster and a half.'

Robison-Greene applies Beauvoir to the show's women. Powerful men are the One and women (like Chalky's community under the Klan) are made the inessential Other, and Beauvoir's apparatus - bad faith, the 'appeal' free beings must make to one another, and the happiness that lets women be complicit in their own oppression - frames Lucy, Gillian, and Margaret. Lucy happily performs the role her men write for her, Gillian is so consumed by the fact of her rape that even her apparent freedom keeps her the object of male desire ('just the loneliest person on earth'), while Margaret - Temperance Leaguer, advocate for women's reproductive health, and finally the woman who shuts the door on Nucky's cash - comes closest to making the appeal and to freedom.

Archibald reads Gillian through Plato's Phaedo. The Argument of Opposites - cyclical deaths and rebirths that the immortal soul survives - maps onto the rape at thirteen that killed the child pageant girl and birthed a survivor, her shift into caretaker to control the stroked-out Commodore, and her final drugged regression before Nucky ('Nucky he did something very bad to me'). The Theory of Forms explains her treatment of roles as interchangeable: Jimmy is son, lover, and husband-Form rather than a person to mourn, Angela's death is merely an opportunity for rebirth, and the Jimmy-lookalike Roger can be dressed with his dog tags as 'James' - Forms changing shape while remaining, to Gillian, undamaged.

Mellamphy uses Zizek's Violence to divide the show's bloodshed - Jimmy's hijacking shootout, Eli's wrench murder of O'Neill, Rosetti burning Sheriff Sickels alive - as subjective violence whose spectacle distracts from objective violence: symbolic (the Klan's racism, the language of the Muhammad caricature controversy) and systemic (the capitalism that keeps Nucky untouchable). Zizek's 'chocolate laxative' logic - ruthless exploitation masked by charity - captures 'I'm a philanthropist now' answered by 'You're a gangster. Plain and simple,' and the opening credits' shifting sea shows Nucky's dual roles merging. Critics who complain about gore see only subjective violence and miss the system that produces it, exactly as Zizek predicts, with Marx's self-enhancing circulation of capital as the unseen engine.

Cobb treats the show's storytellers as narrative pedagogues. Nucky's wharf-rat speech is story truth rather than happening truth - Plato's Republic question of true and false tales - and because it allows no dialogue or questioning it fails as full pedagogy; Chalky's story of his father's lynching ties past to present in the interrogation of the Klansman; Rothstein's billiard-ball anecdote for Frankie Yale is episodic memory shaped into identity and threat, a coerced but genuine reasoning exchange ('Do you know what the moral is of this tale, Mr. Yale?'). Measured against Socrates' question-posing inquiry in the Euthyphro, Kant's On Education, and Freire's dialogical 'critical co-investigators,' Nucky, Chalky, and Rothstein all emerge as reflective but deficient pedagogues at large.

holes.name: Sigmund Freud
holes.what: Founder of psychoanalysis: the id/ego/superego structural model, the Eros versus Thanatos contest, repression, the Oedipus complex, and civilization as built on renounced instinct.
holes.why: Chapter 14 reads Van Alden's eruptions, the audience's identification with Nucky and Jimmy, and the Jimmy-Gillian incest as Oedipal primal-horde parricide entirely through Freud, but he is absent from the taxonomy.

holes.name: Ethics of Docudrama (reel history vs real history)
holes.what: The applied-ethics question of when it is wrong to blend fact with fiction in historical drama that viewers may take as fact.
holes.why: Chapter 17 argues Boardwalk Empire's inaccuracies about Capone, McGarrigle, and Atlantic City's bloodless corruption unethically mislead viewers who 'learn' the false history, a gap the taxonomy's deception-free concept list does not cover.

holes.name: John Calvin
holes.what: Protestant reformer whose Institutes teach a radical doctrine of divine omnipotence: every event, including death, is determined by God's decree.
holes.why: Chapter 18 grounds Van Alden's strong providential theology in Calvin's determinism, quoting the Institutes directly to drive the problem of evil, yet Calvin is missing from the taxonomy.

holes.name: Doing vs Allowing Harm
holes.what: The debated doctrine, classically argued through active versus passive euthanasia, that actively causing a harm is morally worse than merely enabling or allowing it.
holes.why: Chapter 19's entire assessment of Nucky's blame for Gillian's rape, and Jimmy's right to blame him, turns on whether enabling and failing to stop harm is as wrong as causing it, a distinction the taxonomy lacks.

holes.name: The Ethics of Lying and Deception
holes.what: The moral analysis of lying: Kant's absolute ban, Grotius's life-saving exceptions, Bok on trust, and Sorensen's bald-faced lies that are not intended to deceive.
holes.why: Chapter 20 is wholly devoted to which bootleggers' lies are wrong - altruistic lies, lies to the willing, lies to liars, bald-faced lies - and the taxonomy has no concept naming lying or deception.

holes.name: The Body Politic
holes.what: The ancient-to-early-modern metaphor of the state as a living organism whose ruler is the head and whose citizens are the parts, as in Seneca's De Clementia and Hobbes's Leviathan frontispiece.
holes.why: Chapter 22 reads Nucky's hygiene obsession, Prohibition's purity politics, and Nucky-as-king entirely through the body politic metaphor, which the taxonomy's political concepts do not include.

holes.name: Slavoj Zizek
holes.what: Continental philosopher whose Violence distinguishes visible subjective violence from objective violence - symbolic (language, racism) and systemic (the invisible coercion of capitalism).
holes.why: Chapter 29 is an extended application of Zizek's subjective/objective violence distinction to the show's gore and to Nucky's philanthropy-cum-racketeering, but Zizek is absent from the taxonomy.

holes.name: Paulo Freire
holes.what: Brazilian critical pedagogue whose Pedagogy of the Oppressed holds that true education requires dialogue among 'critical co-investigators' rather than one-way imposition.
holes.why: Chapter 30 leans on Freire's dialogue and problem-posing criteria to judge Nucky's, Chalky's, and Rothstein's storytelling as deficient pedagogy, but Freire is absent from the taxonomy.
